name: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah
bio: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah was a chief, with his elder brother Malik, of the Yarbu' branch of Tamim. Malik was put to death by Khalid ibn al-Walid after the fight at al-Butah in A.H. 11, and Mutammim lamented him in elegies, among them Ode LXVII; Ode IX is also attributed to Malik himself.
Lyall explains that 'Mutammim' is properly a title from the game of Maisir, designating a man who takes on several portions of a slaughtered camel.

poems.title: Ode IX: Zunaibah has severed the bond that
poems.author: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Mutammim son of Nuwairah, of Yarbu', of Tamim. Lyall notes that the poem is also frequently attributed to Mutammim's elder brother Malik.
poems.text:
Zunaibah has severed the bond that joined her to one who, for his part, cuts not the bonds that bind him to those he loves ; and truly, sore is the wound she deals to good faith !

And in sooth I yearned for a little kindness from her on that day of parting : but [all that I gained was] her eyes swimming in tears unshed.

Cut then thy bonds, O Zunaibah : as for me, I have been singled out to suffer from a tie to one who is wont to break all ties.

Yea, in sooth I cut the bond on the day when no hope was left for it more — and he who comes to a quick decision in affairs is the man of purpose and resolve —

With a fleet she-camel, strong and sturdy, whose hump is like a castle raised high, built by Nabataeans working briskly thereon.

She spent the summer in Uthal as far as al-Mala, and the spring she passed in the rugged Highland, grazing far afield, becoming plump and round, laid aside from all work ;

Until, when she became with foal, and there had grown up upon her a hump covered with matted wool, the steepness of which made the raven fear to alight thereon,

I brought her near to the saddle, what time there came upon me a journey I needs must make, and a fixed purpose to fulfil ;

Then thou wouldst have thought her, after long weary travel through the night, a strong wild-ass, by whose side gallops, vying with him, a shy she-ass, with marks of pregnancy plain in her.

He keeps her away from her foal, and she keeps him off from herself : verily, the orphan is thrust from one to another !

Day-long he watches over her like a scout, erect, upstanding, on the top of a rising-ground, and hardly does he graze at all ;

Till at last she is driven down to water, on the evening of the fourth day, by a stout sturdy mate speeding on behind her.

He gallops, while his lusty mate races with him over the broken mountainous ground, shooting ahead as the well-bucket darts downwards when its rope is frayed through and gives way.

When at last the two come down to the springs, .over which are tangles of long reeds, some shooting up, and others trampled down,

He lights upon Safwan crouching down by the side of the pool, in his hunter's shelter, all intent on a quarry.

Then the man shot at the she-ass, and missed her: the arrow struck upon a stone, and its point was broken and its shaft splintered.

When she turned in terror, her mate, braying loudly, made swiftly for her, to shield her rear from danger, as a valiant warrior plunges into the fight in defence of his kin ;

Then she smites him on the throat with her hoof and with the hard stones [cast backwards as she flies], and gallops away without restraint.

There is nothing that matches his handling of her, when he mounts her back, and his head reaches forward over her.

Yea, and oft-times have I gone forth in the morning to hunt, my comrade a steed stout in the sides, a pourer-forth of running, of mighty frame,

With bushy hair in his forelock and tail, as though he shook in the air a bunch of moist swamp-grass as often as he is checked in his gallop,

Full of keenness when thou lettest him go, throwing himself forward, eager to run heat after heat whenever he is reined in.

When he gallops in the race past the shouting groups of men, stretching his neck and reaching forward his head, he is like an oryx beset on both sides by dogs, bending down his head [to pierce them with his horns].

I trained him and fed him up with all possible care, and I gave him as much attention as a wealthy man gives to his dearest friend.

He gets the collected milk of many she-camels whose milk [through pregnancy] has become scanty — all but a small residue; and his blanket is not taken off while he is carefully tended in the tent.

Then, when we race our horses together, he is always the first, out-stripping all : his rider goes proudly when he is started in every contest.

Yea, many the day we have appointed the stakes he has won to be spent in gifts and loans for life to friends, and so have we been profitable to them.

And oft-times have I been beforehand with the railing women by draining a deep draught of wine in the morning, while my wine-jug was large and brimming —

A growth of black grapes, pure in colour, deep red like the blood of a victim of sacrifice when it is poured forth, mixed with water ;

I rejoice therein on a day, and I bring joy to a band of friends, causing them to forget their troubles what time they have been wrapped up and hooded therein.

Woe 's me for the long-maned creature, with tufts of hair on her neck, that comes to me limping on three legs !

She watches me through the day and looks about her : the spark of life that is left in me gives her pause, but it is I she craves for ;

She will spend the day tearing me to pieces and feeding her cubs with my flesh, in the midst of her covert — and no living soul will lift a hand to drive her off.

If only my sword were in my hand, I would smite her with it and repel her, so that I should not be devoured by her while I lie defenceless :

Yea, time was when I smote with it, and my stroke used to strike off the hands of the warriors as though they were stems of soft wood.

This it is to perish [ — not the wasting of my goods] ! Therefore, O railer, if I cut off my hand with a knife, say — ' What he does is well done !'

And oft was I envied for a season for the good luck that was my lot — and then again follows thereon a day that is hateful :

But after those have gone that Nusaibah bore shall I complain of the shears of Doom, or be seen lamenting what needs must be ?

And of a truth I know — and there is no averting it — that I am destined to be the sport of Fate : but dost thou see me wailing thereat ?

Fate brought to nought 'Ad, then the race of Muharriq, and has left them, and all that they brought together, a bare, desolate plain :

Yea, Destiny has destroyed both the Hariths, and has reft away the Tubba', the master of great fortresses.

I too count my ancestors back to the root of the Earth : and I summon them, but I know that they will not hear.

They have gone their way, and I cannot overtake them : Destruction has called them, and they have betaken themselves to her, and the broad Way that all must tread.

There is no escape from the stroke of Doom : await it then ; whether in the land of thine own people or in another thou shalt be laid low ;

And in due time shall come upon thee a day when there shall be weeping over thee, while thou liest in thy shroud and hearest not.

poems.title: Ode LXVII: It is not my wont to
poems.author: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah
poems.text:
It is not my wont to chant the praises of one who dies, or utter the cry of woe beneath pain that Fortune brings :

But, sooth, he whom al-Minhal enshrouded as dead he lay — no glutton at eve was he, a warrior keen of heart!

No niggard, to whose wife bring the women their offerings, what time in the winter wind the tent of stiff leather creaks :

A wise man, but one whose wisdom hindered not generous hand : a pasture of plenty to which in famine the starvelings flocked.

Thou sawest him, keen as a sword, most eager and quick to give, whenas men of dull cold heart spent nothing to stay thy need ;

And if on a day thy foes beset thee with stifling press, if he was thine aid, thy cause was not that which lost the fight ;

And if mid the roystering band thou earnest on Malik there, no foul speech or cross-grained word he uttered, nor stirred up strife ;

And if on the tribe a raid fell sudden and sharp, 'twas he that stood in defence as keen, a glorious chief of men.

Not he to hold back, what time the cavalry wavered and blenched : no weakling in fight, none thrust him aside as of no account.

Not blunt were his weapons when the enemy met his steel in light-equipped ranks on foot, or clad in full panoply.

Nay, why weep ye not, mine eyes, for Malik, when howls the wind and casts down the wattled screen that shelters the cowering herds:

When drinkers assemble : when the need comes for one to stand a champion fit to face the bravest of all our foes :

When seeking for tents at night the guest makes his camel roar : when captives have lain in bonds till shrunken and stiff their limbs :

When brings in her need the widow her starveling shag-pate child, its head like a bustard's chick with feathers all disarrayed?

When forth from their bag men brought the arrows, and heaped the fire with faggots, 'twas he that bore the charge when the partners failed ;

And so, when the game went on, not he one to stint the meat, or sit by the offal where the butchers cut up the joints.

Whereso falls my gaze, I see what thrills me, and shatters all my patience — with Malik gone, an end of all bonds for me!

I call thee — no answer comes ! ah, when did I call before upon thee for help, and missed the cheer of thy quick reply?

Ay, goodly our twinned life! yet before us the stroke of Doom has fallen on mighty kings, on Kisra and Himyar's Lord.

Long fared we like those twain, King Jadhimah's two boon-fellows, so close-knit that none could think that parting would ever come:

But now are we sundered, and it seems as though Malik's hand, for all the long days of love, had ne'er lain a night in mine !

And if now between us Fate has set up the wall of Death, at least, when my brother went, he carried with him fair fame !

I say, while the flashes light the cloud-fringe below the black, and down from the dark mass pours the rain in a scattering flood :

' May God grant the land where lies the grave of my brother dear the blessing of showers at dawn, and cover the ground with green,

' And bring to the Twin Dales' torrent water to fill its stream shall feed the first sprouting grass, and lift it up lush and strong!

' May floods stand about the skirts of Shari', and may the rain soak well all the mountain-sides of Dalfa' and Qaryatan ! '

It is not because I love the land that I pray this boon, but only that rain may quicken the earth where my Darling lies.

A greeting from me to him, though his body lies far away and crumbles to dust, while above the waste stretches void and bare.

The Daughter of 'Amrites asks — ' What ails thee, thou who but now wast cheerful and glad of heart, and tossedst thy flowing hair?'

I answered her : ' Long grieving, the burning of loss within — what wouldst thou? — has left my face dark, stript of all comeliness:

'The loss of my mother's sons who trod one the other's steps to death: yet I stoop not after them, nor abase myself.

'Not I one, when Fortune strikes some new stroke of bitter loss, to burden my kinsfolk, humbling myself to beg for their help ;

' Nor, if on a day some turn of Fate brings prosperity, exult I, nor, when it goes, mourn I or lament the change.

' No ! straight do I tread my path and forward press on my way, though many there" be who shrink and cower in face of fight.

'Yea, though thou canst jest, and I answer lightly, a weight of woe has stricken me, well might bring the hardest to melt in tears.

'The change which thou seest was wrought by that which destroyed my kin-together they fell — Qais, Malik, 'Amr, on Mushaqqar's Day —

' And that which destroyed Yazid, my comrade and boon-fellow — ah, would that with wealth or kin I could buy back his company !

'So prithee, in God's name, stay the burthen of thy reproach, and strip not the half-healed skin to torture again my heart.

' Enough ! I was present there — but nought could I find to do whereby with my hands to turn from them the assault of Doom.'

If that which I suffer had befallen Mutali's mount or Salma's far-spreading base, they surely had crumbled down !

And no, not the bitter pain when three foster-camels find the place where their nurseling, dragged to ground, was devoured by wolves —

They call to the mourner's mind the grief that lies hid within : one leads with her cry, then all join voices in wailing loud ;

The oldest of them stands plaining, trilling her yearning cry : her grief makes the whole herd weep, and spreads through the couching line —

No greater that than my pain the day that my Malik died, and one clear of voice proclaimed our parting for evermore.

Has nought reached your chief men's ears of the doings of al-Muhill — a tidings, in sooth, to anger any with heart to feel! —

How evil his joy when death fell sudden on Malik's head, how there he stood by, and left uncared-for the thing he saw?

Thou broughtest thy ragged clout and stuffed camel-cushion home, and couldst not spare them for Malik's corse, but didst haste away.

One day mayst thou have no joy with that which befalls thyself! for Death, see, impends o'er all, and most o'er the valiant man.

Mayhap an Event one day shall draw nigh to thee, a Thing shall leave thee with nose cropped, earless, facing the scorn of men.

Thou toldest us of his death who, had it been thy flesh lay before him, had given it rest, whole were it or mangled sore.

May Malik's decease bring no good luck to the back-biters ! Who hated him, safe came home, and left the dead lying there.

poems.title: Ode LXVIII: I lay awake, while those free
poems.author: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah
poems.text:
I lay awake, while those free from care slept ; and there stirred up with the coming-on of night a painful grief in my heart ;

And the thought of Malik wakened again my sorrow, and I slept not but with a disturbed heart.

Time after time, when I restrained my tears, they refused to be held back, but gushed forth, tears upon tears,

Like the overflowing of a great water-bag between the side-pieces that confine the pulley, the water of which irrigates the small channels, and the crops [drink it in] —

A water-bag with patches [over the loops] lately sewn on, with its leather full of holes, kept off from the side of the well-shaft by a protuberance in the barrel of the shallow well —

At the remembrance of a loved one which holds me when a good portion of the night is gone, and already is near the coming-forth of the late-rising stars.

When mine eyes are dried of their tears, memory of him is revived in me by the doves that call to one another, alighting on the branches over my head :

They call on their youngling lost, and I am plunged into grief for Malik, and in my breast is a heart cloven with anguish at the thought of him :

It seems as though I had never sat by his side, never seen him by me of a night, never found him there when the morning dawned !

A man he who never lived a day under reproach, and never ceased to have about him encampments of those who sought his bounty ;

A following he always had, for men knew that to those who drew nigh to him he was like the showers of summer and spring

When the milch-camels of the tribe come home at night famine-stricken, driven in by a north-wind that wrinkles the faces and blackens the skin.

When one who had on him the burden of guilt made for the tent of Malik, there stood surety for him a protector high-nosed, a stout defender.

By my life ! goodly was the man when a guest arrived in the late darkness, when there had sped of the longest winter's night something less than a half,

Ready to give freely all that he had in his possession, no niggard, what time hunger bared to day the white-skinned women that thrill men's hearts with their beauty,

What time the Sun in the heaven, in the droughty air, looked like a yellow [disc] with streaks of saffron drawn across it.
